segments.t: Gabriel urges Sandrine Kiberlain to star in a prestigious new period biopic by Daniele Thompson. But Sandrine is tired of crying on screen and secretly dreams of doing stand-up comedy instead. Let's listen to their conversation in French first.
Sandrine, tu as lu ce grand scénario?
Je ne veux plus de drames tristes.
Danièle Thompson propose un rôle magnifique!
Je préfère faire rire le public.
Tu veux monter sur scène seule?
La comédie me donne une énergie folle.
Mais c'est un métier très difficile.
Justement, ce projet nouveau me plaît beaucoup.
Et le tournage du film historique?
Dis-leur que je suis indisponible.
Les producteurs attendent pourtant ta réponse rapide.
J'ai déjà décroché une première partie!
Tu vas vraiment jouer cinq minutes?
Oui, prépare-toi pour mon spectacle!
Let's explore Sandrine and Gabriel's humorous debate line by line.
Sandrine, tu as lu ce grand scénario?
'Sandrine, did you read this great script?' Gabriel asks if she reviewed the prestigious period biopic. This conversational past tense combines a helper verb with the past participle for 'read'.
Je ne veux plus de drames tristes.
'I do not want sad dramas anymore.' Sandrine rejects repetitive tragic film roles. The two-part negative structure wraps around 'want' to express 'no longer' or 'not anymore'.
Danièle Thompson propose un rôle magnifique!
'Daniele Thompson offers a magnificent role!' Gabriel emphasizes the prestige of the director. Notice how 'offers' leads directly into the noun meaning 'role'.
Je préfère faire rire le public.
'I prefer to make the audience laugh.' Sandrine reveals her newfound desire for comedy. The verb meaning 'prefer' pairs naturally with the noun for 'audience.' in everyday conversation.
Tu veux monter sur scène seule?
'You want to go on stage alone?' Gabriel is shocked by her sudden comedy ambition. The adjective meaning 'alone?' takes its feminine form here to match the noun it describes.
La comédie me donne une énergie folle.
'Comedy gives me crazy energy.' Sandrine describes the rush of live humor. The reflexive pronoun sits right in front of the verb for 'gives', turning the action back onto the subject.
Mais c'est un métier très difficile.
'But it is a very difficult trade.' Gabriel warns her of the harsh stage world. The key noun here means 'trade', anchored by its matching French article.
Justement, ce projet nouveau me plaît beaucoup.
'Precisely, this new project pleases me a lot.' Sandrine welcomes the fresh artistic challenge. The verb meaning 'pleases' pairs naturally with the noun for 'project' in everyday conversation.
Et le tournage du film historique?
'And the shoot of the historical film?' Gabriel worries about letting down the production team. The descriptive adjective for 'historical?' agrees in gender and number with its noun.
Dis-leur que je suis indisponible.
'Tell them that I am unavailable.' Sandrine firmly turns down the period biopic. The descriptive adjective for 'unavailable.' agrees in gender and number with its noun.
Les producteurs attendent pourtant ta réponse rapide.
'The producers expect your prompt reply though.' Gabriel stresses mounting commercial pressure. Gabriel uses the casual singular 'you' with 'expect', showing close familiarity.
J'ai déjà décroché une première partie!
'I already landed an opening act!' Sandrine proudly announces her upcoming stage debut. The adjective meaning 'first' takes its feminine form here to match the noun it describes.
Tu vas vraiment jouer cinq minutes?
'Are you really going to perform five minutes?' Gabriel realizes that her mind is completely made up. Notice how 'are going' leads directly into the noun meaning 'minutes?'.
Oui, prépare-toi pour mon spectacle!

'Yes, get ready for my show!' Sandrine invites him to see her live performance. Dropping the subject pronoun turns the verb for 'prepare' into a direct, punchy command. Now let's listen to Sandrine and Gabriel's complete discussion once again.
